utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, you are to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, good morning Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Mr. Mandic. I trust you've been able to rest last night. I want to start by asking you some questions about the brigade, the 1st Sarajevo mechanised brigade and I want to ask you, isn't it the case that the Sarajevo mechanised brigade was called that -- was given that name because it was unique in terms of the mechanical facilities it had and the weapons it had. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 1st Sarajevo Brigade, as far as I know, was just called the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, not mechanised, and it's true that we had certain combat equipment and as I said, we also had some vehicles for transportation of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, and in fact the 1st Sarajevo or the mechanical brigade had a tank battalion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the tank battalion consisted of armoured personnel carriers and armoured vehicles. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The armoured battalion only had tanks, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in addition to the armoured battalion, wasn't there a mixed heavy artillery division which consisted of heavy weapons ranging from 120 to 155-millimetre weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not as part of the battalion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But there was a mixed heavy artillery division, at least within the Sarajevo brigade, mechanised brigade. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was artillery, that is true. However, I don't know if it was whether in part of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade or whether it was part of some other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in any case, if required, as you said yesterday, if required, the -- the Sarajevo mechanised brigade and the battalions within that brigade were able to draw upon artillery support during combat?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, you are again saying the 1st Sarajevo mechanised brigade. It was the 1st Sarajevo brigade. It's true that we asked for assistance and help from other brigades in case of danger for the civilian population. Of course a large loss of personnel would mean that we asked for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in addition to the -- well, in addition to your battalion, the logistics battalion there were also, as I understand it, four other battalions within the Sarajavo brigade, the 1st Sarajevo brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, we had in our battalion a company, this company for the maintenance of wheeled motor vehicles. We had a company for the procurement of fuel and we also had a medical unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps -- I was actually asking you about the brigade and the number of battalions within the brigade. And my understanding is that there were four battalions in addition to the logistics battalion within the brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot give you a specific and correct answer about that, because I really don't know how many brigades the battalion had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I take it you mean you don't know how many battalions the brigade had. Is that what you said? Because the translation came out differently.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Apart from the times that you were wounded, I understand that you remained within the Sarajevo -- 1st Sarajevo Brigade throughout the conflict. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you were also aware that there was a military police battalion within the Sarajevo brigade, the 1st Sarajevo Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the military police battalion, I suggest to you that one of the purposes of this battalion would be to -- if there were errant soldiers, or if there were crimes committed, the persons from this battalion would be involved in any investigation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. If any soldier of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade would commit something wrong, he would be detained by the police and of course that soldier would be subject to an appropriate punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and his brigade commander, Mr. Stojanovic of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, had -- if needed, had the means to conduct investigations into crimes that may have been committed by their soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In your time with the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, the Sarajevo Brigade are you aware of any investigations that were conducted into crimes committed by soldiers? In other words, the targeting of civilians inside the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question, because I did not take part, nor did I witness the shooting of civilians in Sarajevo. It's true that were investigations and that people were put in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say that it's true there were investigations and people were put in prison, is it your evidence that there were investigations into SRK soldiers committing crimes? In other words, targeting civilians inside the city of Sarajevo. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that the witness should be allowed to answer specifically. He talked about misdemeanours by the soldiers of the army of the Republika Srpska and the Prosecutor keeps insisting on crimes about which he doesn't know anything and he said that several times. He spoke about misdemeanours committed by soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska. Well, he would need to explain that in more detail but at no point did he speak about the kind of crimes that the Prosecutor is asking him about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I don't recollect hearing the word "misdemeanours."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours,, the word misdemeanours or violations is clear, but it's not a crime. These are completely -- two completely different things. In my language, in B/C/S, it's a very clear word. And you can ask the accused to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and I acknowledge the difference between misdemeanours and crimes. What I'm saying is that in the translation, we didn't have the word "misdemeanours." But I'm going ask the witness to explain what he means when he said, "It is true there were investigations and that people were put in prison." What was investigated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade punished members of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade for violations, for such as if there were any looting, running away from the line, not responding in time to the summons to return to the unit after a leave of a few days, this is the sort of thing that I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you -- there would have been investigations into violations such as looting and failing to report after taking leave of absence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for drunkenness and cases like that. These would be misdemeanours or violations which are quite normal after two or three years, when people would tend to start behaving that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, sir, I take it, then, to your knowledge there was never an investigation into -- an investigation into the conduct by Sarajevo-Romanija Corps soldiers for targeting civilians inside the city?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm repeating once more that I did not have the opportunity to see firing at or the suffering of the civilian population in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer, but my question was somewhat different. I just want you to tell the Court whether you are aware during your time in the 1st Sarajevo Brigade of any investigations into alleged conduct by Sarajevo-Romanija Corps soldiers whereby civilians were targeted. If you're not aware of any investigation, just say so.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know about firing at the Sarajevo civilians even. And I don't know about any investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I understand that your role within the logistics battalion, in that role you would have had a fair amount of knowledge of the -- let's say the working functions or the operations of the other battalions within the brigade. Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. You are not right. I told you yesterday that we received reports about attacks on the front lines, about the force of the attacks, if help was necessary, and if it was we were sent to those locations that needed assistance in order to hold the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But as your -- in your job within the battalion, you would have known about the relative situation with respect to ammunition within the battalions or in respect to the fuel within the battalions. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you're saying that your job within the logistics battalion, you knew nothing about the level of ammunition within the other battalions within your brigade. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, in that case, I take it you really can't comment on whether the other battalions had heavy weapons and other such ammunition. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wasn't informed about the quantity of ammunition. Since I worked as a vehicle electrician and I would go out into the field to repair vehicles, so I was able to find out about the type of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So now I'm -- I'm starting to get confused. Are you -- would you be aware of whether the other battalions in your brigade had, for example, 82-millimetre mortars, 120-millimetre mortars, Howitzers and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't have the opportunity to see the weapons. As you know, that kind of weapon is deployed by military strategists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So then I take it that you do not know whether, in the period October -- well, in the period of 1994, 1995 whether the other battalions had 82-millimetre mortars, 120-millimetre mortars. That's something you do not know, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time all the heavy weapons, as I said yesterday, were concentrated in warehouses of the Slobodan Princip Seljo barracks and the blue helmets were there 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that answer, but my suggestion to you is that irrespective of whether the weapons were at the barracks, you don't know whether the other battalions deployed such weapons along their territory, because, as you've told the Court, that's not something within your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that according to the decision of our leadership of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Sarajevo-Romanija region in agreement with I don't know who, the heavy weapons were pulled back and placed under the surveillance of the blue helmets. After that, I didn't hear the firing from our side of any artillery weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you're saying the Sarajevo-Romanija region, are you talking about the region within your brigade or throughout -- throughout the region of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that there was an order for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. As far as we're concerned, the 1st Sarajevo Battalion, all the weapons were pulled back to depots, and then later they were pulled out of an exclusion zone of 20 kilometres, outside the Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And how did you know about this order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard about it from our officers and I saw when our heavy weapons, the tanks, transporters, the heavy weaponry, was brought near the technical workshop where I used to perform my maintenance duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that's when the weapons were removed from the area of the battalions; you weren't there at that time to see the removal of the weapon, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was able to see when the tanks and the other heavy weaponry was taken away, accompanied or escorted by the blue helmets and then later I found out that the blue helmets had ordered that the weapons be pulled out 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo, and they were taken to some locations at Jahorina and other places that the blue helmets chose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, let's try and be precise here. Are you saying that when the weapons were taken away from the battalions within your brigade that you were there at the time that they were removed, you were there with the officers, the UNPROFOR officers with blue helmets. Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was an answer to the same question two or three times and then it is still being insisted on the same question. I mean, we can go on like this indefinitely. If you give an answer to a question two or three times then I don't understand the purpose of it. So I object to this manner of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, generally, Mr. Sachdeva, I think you tend to repeat the questions, but in this instance I believe it is permissible. Answer the question, Witness. Because counsel is allowed to clarify the questions and to seek a clarification of the answers that he has -- that have been given. Counsel is allowed to probe, Mr. Tapuskovic. But I agree, that where a clear answer has been given, the question should not be asked again. In this instance, the witness is to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question. I was not with the UN officers at that point of time. I wasn't with the officers of the army of Republika Srpska either. But I did see, because the technical workshop is only 50 metres away from the warehouse where the tanks and the weaponry was being stored. I could see when they left, because the tanks had to pass along the road near the workshop. So I saw them when they were leaving, when they were pulling out to 20 kilometres away from the exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But it's correct, is it not, that did you not see the 120-millimetre mortars or the 82-millimetre mortars being removed from areas within the 3 or 4 battalions of the brigade. You did not see that take place, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When the personnel carriers and tanks were pulling out and when the 150-millimetre weapons were being driven away, covered by tarpaulins, I think that perhaps the mortars were also being taken away. I'm not sure. But there were a lot of such weapons so I assume that all of these weapons were being pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, firstly, I take it then it's an assumption on your part, is that right, that they were removed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. But, excuse me, only if we're talking about mortars, because mortars have to be transported on vehicles. They cannot be moved without vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. So your assumption is that the mortars were removed from the areas of the battalion. It's not something you know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that when the weapons were taken back to the barracks, the Slobodan Princip barracks, these weapons were malfunctioning and were out of order. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. For the simple reason that I know that all the tanks were pulled back to the hangars and because the blue helmets knew we had a technical workshop which was split into two for the repair of wheeled vehicles and Caterpillar vehicles. And when the blue helmets were there, we had two tanks and one BRD on repair, and every day, they would come at least five or six times to inspect the tanks and the personnel carrier to make sure that it hadn't gone anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I want to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 03149 brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, sir, you're aware that the TEZ, the exclusion zone agreement, was signed on or around the 9th or 8th of September -- 8th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would kindly ask for a hard copy again for me to me to be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But can you first answer the question, that the TEZ agreement was signed around -- on or around the 8th or 9th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not memorise the date. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But roughly at that time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As a plain soldier, I wasn't in a position to worry about such things, for example, when agreements were signed. My primary concern was to safe the lives of he members of my family and my children rather than worrying about when agreements were signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you are aware, are you not, that the reason for the -- this agreement, the reason why this agreement came into force was because of the incident at the Markale market on the 5th of February, 1994. Is that something that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know of Markale. However, I also know about other speculations concerning Markale. You know of Russian colonel who tried to explain that no shell could have landed there. He was sent back to Russia, although he was a member of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. If I want further information, I'll ask you. I simply want you to tell the Court that you are aware that there was an incident at the marketplace on the 5th of February, 1994, where civilians were killed. You're aware of that incident, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now in this document that you're reading, you'll see that -- that it emanates from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command. You see that at the top there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, commands of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps at Lukavica, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: 10 of February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see that it is -- it is being sent or it has been sent to the Main Staff and the attention is to General Milovanovic. You see that there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the title or the subject matter is the proposal for setting aside artillery. You can read that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if you look at the first paragraph it is explained, I suggest to you, that this is a proposal to -- a proposal put forward by General Milosevic to ensure that even with the agreement, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps would not have to set aside all its heavy weaponry. You see at the end of the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't see General Milosevic mentioned anywhere. What I see here is General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'll show you General Milosevic's signature at the end of the document. But I just want you to concentrate on the first paragraph. And in particular this sentence. You see that it says: "In addition, upon the implementation of this proposal, the SRK forces would not suffer any damages and would not be left without equipment since we would use a diversionary tactic to set aside the equipment that is out of order and for which we do not have sufficient quantities of ammunition." You see that in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see where it states the proposal is the following.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it says, "From the area of responsibility of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade," which is your brigade, I understand, "we would set aside in total 16 artillery pieces, out of which ten have been received from the Herzegovina Corps and are out of order." And in brackets it says 2 Howitzers, 105-millimetre, three 76-metre field guns, 2 anti-tank guns one PAT anti-aircraft gun and one 120-millimetre mortar. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So it's clear, isn't it, from this document, that the map was to remove the weapons that were non-functioning and weapons which -- which -- for which there was not sufficient ammunition, but to, I suggest to you, but to keep the heavy weapons in the field that would still provide support to the SRK?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't see them, and I know nothing of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So your evidence about whether the weapons were removed and the weapons being stored at the barracks is not totally correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is absolutely correct that I saw our tanks leave from the hangar next to the workshop in the direction of Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so you don't know, do you, that there was a plan to camouflage other heavy weapons in the area of the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, so as to -- so as to -- to fall foul of the UNPROFOR monitoring. In other words, UNPROFOR would not be able to monitor these weapons that were camouflaged?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that UNPROFOR had no restrictions of movement. They had access everywhere. Their soldiers moved about residential areas inhabited by civilians. I know specifically that my children, too, would run away upon seeing them, because that was the amount of fear that by that time was in any civilian or a child when seeing any other soldier other than a VRS soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to go to the last page of this document. And I just want you to confirm that that is the -- you will see there that is signed by the deputy commander, Colonel Dragomir Milosevic. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P802, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in -- I'm finished with the document, so you could -- you can put the document down. Yesterday when answering questions -- answering the questions of Mr. Tapuskovic, the -- counsel asked you when the general, General Milosevic came into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic, did you wish to see that document? You were gesticulating and I was trying to understand the gesticulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have that document here. I wanted to ask for the document to remain with the witness since I will have additional questions on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Yes, please. Let the document be passed back to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, General Milosevic took over the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on around August 1994. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And yesterday Mr. Tapuskovic asked you after August 1994 what those first few months were like, and you answered: "We were issued an order then. It wasn't a prohibition, but an order that we were not permitted to fire from infantry or artillery weapons until mid-October, from what I can remember." You remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do, but I don't think that is exactly the way I put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I'll read the question. Then I'll read you the answer. The question was: "And the first" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic. Did you wish to say something, Mr. Tapuskovic, or will you allow counsel to put the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will allow the counsel, since my objection had to do with that. If we put it to the witness, if we put what he said yesterday to him, then the question is all right. If Mr. Sachdeva intends to show him exactly what it is that he said, then there is no need for me to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, what I asked you just a moment ago was what I was reading from the transcript yesterday at page 63 and the question was, "And the first months when he arrived, what were they like, the months from August on and then until the end of 1994?" That was the question. And your answer, and I quote: "We were issued an order then. It wasn't a prohibition, but an order that we were not permitted to fire from infantry or artillery weapons from mid-October, from what I can remember." That was your answer. Do you remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember the answer, but the idea was not conveyed. What I said was that between August until mid-October it was quiet, and that we were given express orders not to use either infantry or artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so what I want to ask you is that after October when -- when maybe it wasn't so quiet, were you then permitted whether in retaliation or in other circumstances, were you then permitted to fire, to use infantry and artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: By the end of October, there may have been some provocations at the front lines. At first, they were sporadic and then they intensified. We had to respond by using infantry weapons, unless we failed to do that, we would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you responded by infantry weapons. Did you also, or not necessarily just you, but your colleagues also respond with artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, there was no artillery at the front lines, particularly not in Dobrinja IV where I was. What was there was infantry and infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I used word "artillery" because you mentioned it yesterday in your answer. So let me put it this way. Even if there was not artillery at the front lines, if required, artillery support could have been called for, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We didn't need any artillery in a residential area. We were separated by a street only. Therefore, there was no use of any artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So why did you mention artillery yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mentioned artillery because it was an express order, and I repeat an express order not to fire from either infantry or artillery weapons. That is what we were said. It was also said that we were not even to use a slingshot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the order with respect to infantry fire and artillery weapons, presumably, artillery weapons included mortars, 82-millimetre mortars, 120-millimetre mortars, Howitzers, tanks, that's how you understood the order. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I can't say that only those represent artillery. There's also anti-aircraft artillery. Anything beyond 12 millimetres is artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But artillery would also include tanks and 120 and 80-millimetre mortars. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but also what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I understand that. So if, as you've testified today, all the heavy weapons were removed, why would there be a need for an order not to fire from these weapons, if they did not exist on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The order was issued in its entirety, meaning that no combat activity was to be conducted at the front lines facing the enemy. That was the overall idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. You're not actually answering my question. You have given evidence today that all the heavy weapons were removed after the TEZ agreement, and I'm suggesting to you that an order that you are aware of that called for -- that called on you and your soldiers not to fire from artillery and infantry weapons suggests, doesn't it, that indeed artillery weapons were not removed and they still were in use?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. To repeat yet again, the order was that we must not attack the enemy front lines by using either infantry or artillery weapons, not even with slingshots. We were not even allowed to cast a stone, let alone anything else. That was the way I understood it, and that was the order that was conveyed to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not disputing what the order said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, you have explored this point sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, earlier today I was asking you about the battalions within your brigade, and can you confirm that there was within one of the battalions a specialised sniping detachment within the Sarajevo -- the 1st Sarajevo Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 1st Sarajevo Brigade, I claim it with full responsibility, did not have a single sharpshooter, let alone an entire detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, there were no snipers or soldiers with rifles positioned at the shopping buildings in Grbavica? You're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were soldiers around with rifles, yes. But there is a distinction or at least it has to be made between a sniper rifle and a regular rifle. For example, I had a rifle, a regular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, within your brigade there was a 2nd Battalion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know this division by battalions. I cannot reply to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: There was a battalion that had in its AOR, area of responsibility, Grbavica and its surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And a very senior soldier within that battalion, the 2nd Battalion, has told -- has given a statement to the ICTY that there was indeed a specialised sniper detachment within the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. Does that cause you to reflect upon your answer earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Again, I can tell you that I never saw or heard a sniper being fired in the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. At least not where I was, which is predominantly in the area of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you ever go to Grbavica during the war as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you don't know, do you, whether there was a sniper detachment in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether it existed, whether such a sniping detachment existed. I know that the road between Sarajevo and Pale was covered by snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When counsel is on his feet, you must stop. What is it, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness answered twice saying he doesn't know. He said that there were none where he was. He said he wasn't at Grbavica, and yet the question is being put for the third time. It goes on, just like it did before. I understand that an issue needs to be cleared up, but if the witness has given a clear answer, saying he didn't know and there were none where he was and that he was not in Grbavica where there might have been some, then that's it. I don't think one needs to insist so many times on the same question to which the witness had already given answers twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I suggest, I submit that I was not repeating my question. I wanted to establish that he was not in Grbavica and therefore I put the logical conclusion that he would not know and he confirmed that, and that's all I need to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you're aware, aren't you, that within the Sarajevo Brigade, there were modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Have you heard of a modified air bomb before, or what a modified air bomb is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what a modified air bomb is. The only time I saw any air bombs was on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You worked in the logistics battalion and you've given evidence about tanks and other weapons, and you're now telling the Court that you have never heard of a modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if air bombs have anything to do with the tanks or the 150 Dites [phoen] or any other wheeled vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, modified air bombs are weapons, aren't they? They're heavy weapons, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I have never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about modified air bombs being used by your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 02584.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, would you like me to provide you a hard copy or are you able to read that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A hard copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You see at the top firstly it says logistics, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I see where it says command of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade and then logistics, yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see that it's signed by the commander of the brigade, Veljko Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that this is a request for an air bomb launcher to be given to the 1st Sarajevo Brigade from the Igman Infantry Brigade. You can see that this is that request, can't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From what I understand here, this was not done at logistics or at the technical workshop of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. But the technical workshop had several sectors, it had locksmiths, mechanics, painters, electrical sections, so everything that was required to maintain vehicles, it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And this document appears to you to be a valid and legitimate document, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Can you just please just allow me to read it properly, because I see that Hadzici is mentioned here and ... This was probably done in the technical and maintenance section of Hadzici, and I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you agree with me that is a request for an air bomb launcher, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P803, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, Witness, I would like to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If 65 ter 02587 could be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I have the hard copy for you. Witness, firstly you will note that the first document I showed you was dated the 20th of August, 1995, and you will see this document is dated the 22nd of August, 1995. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just take a moment to read this document and I'll ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Firstly you'll see that this is signed by Mr. Solar, who was within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command in logistics. You see that there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And there is an order in response to the previous document I showed you, and it is upon the request of the brigade commander, Mr. Stojanovic, it is an order to release an air bomb launcher for the purposes of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. Isn't what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I see the document, but all of this was happening far from Lukavica at the Hadzici technical maintenance facility, and it could be something to do with the Igman Brigade. In any case, I wasn't able to know about these things, because I didn't have the opportunity to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You were in the logistics battalion for the duration of the conflict, weren't you, of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in the technical workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on seeing these two documents is it still your evidence that you know nothing about the use of modified air bombs by your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I still assert that, because they were not used in the area where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I don't see anything wrong with that question. Counsel is allowed to probe. He has put a document and he is entitled to, once again, ascertain whether the witness maintains his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to bother you, Your Honours. I'll have the opportunity to deal with this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P804, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I want to show you another document, and I -- I don't know if I have a hard copy in B/C/S here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In any event, it's 65 ter 03199.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, unfortunately, I don't have a hard copy in your language. Are you able to see on the screen, are you able to read that document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just take a moment to read this document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you'll see that this is an approval for the -- an approval by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command for the issuance of ammunition to the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you'll see that in items 8 and 9, the approval is for 40 pieces of 82-millimetre mortar rounds and 40 pieces of 120-millimetre rounds. You'll see that there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see the date is the 25th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So it's correct, isn't it, Witness, that the heavy weapons, all the heavy weapons were not removed from the brigade, as the agreement stipulated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about a fierce offensive on the Trnovo front here. So I don't know if the mortars came from other brigades, but I say it again, I never saw that the 1st Sarajevo Brigade had heavy weaponry after the pull-out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P805, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I'm finished with the document, so you can put the document down. Are you aware of a location called Ozrenska Street?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you were aware that from that -- at least from certain parts of that street there was a commanding view of the city of Sarajevo, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if I told you that a senior person within the 2nd battalion of your brigade has told the ICTY that there were sniper positions in -- in a house on Ozrenska street, is that something that you would agree with or know about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know that the line in Ozrenska was just -- the lines at Ozrenska were just four to six metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you know that from Ozrenska Street, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps soldiers with rifles would fire into enemy territory, that is, into the lines controlled by the ABiH. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. We opened fire at their front line, meaning when they fired provocation fire or wished to destroy us, then we had to respond. But we would fire at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you ever fire from Ozrenska Street? Did you personally ever fire from Ozrenska Street?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you were situated where in Ozrenska Street? From where did you fire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Miliklanska and Ozrenska intersection, from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And were you in a house, an abandoned house?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. We had dug a trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And from that trench, did you have a view of the city, a commanding view of the Sarajevo city?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From the trench, we could only see four enemy bunkers which were in houses across the road, and while I was there, three fighters of the army of Republika Srpska were killed in that trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How long were you there for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was attached there for about ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How many times? Was it just one time that you were attached there or did you go there more than one time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only once to that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And how many soldiers were with you when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mostly there were two, possibly three, if an attack was expected during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What sort of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We had automatic rifles and black hand grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And these automatic rifles, they had a range of 500 metres. Is that right? Or was it a longer range?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: An automatic rifle has a range of 2.000 metres, but the only thing is it's not precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you're saying that at the very least, one could hit a target 1000 metres away from the rifle you had. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. You could hit a target precisely up to 100 metres, and this by a good marksman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could you not hit a car 500 metres away with that rifle?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't have the opportunity to fire in order to test it. If it was a moving car, then I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not asking whether you yourself fired. I'm suggesting to, actually I'm asking you that within an M48 you could hit a car, whether it was stationery or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You earlier put 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Up to 500 metres, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's not the same thing to fire at a moving or a stationary target.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, let's put it this way: If there was a stationary target, let's say the car had stopped at traffic lights. Up to 500 metres from the rifle you had, that car could be engaged, could it not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. And there were no traffic lights.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: From the position you were in Ozrenska Street you've already said that you had a view of the city. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So what could you see from where you were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Four-storeyed houses, four bunkers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, he has responded for the second time to the same question in the same way. I don't understand why the same thing is being put to him several times. Just before he said that he could just see trenches opposite from him which were four metres away or however he put it and now this is an even more detailed explanation of what he was able to see, but this is a question that is being repeated, but he did say specifically what he was able to see from the trench that he was in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He didn't have a view of the city but he was able to see four-storeyed houses and bunkers. Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you to mark your precise location on a map. Would you be able to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe that I would be able to do that. It's very simple, also for you to find the intersection of the Miliklanska and Ozrenska streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to you do that if you don't mind. Let's see how we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could have the map 2872.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But he says that he doesn't believe that he would be able to do it. So if that answer is to be accepted, how can you ask him to do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, my submission is that he doesn't -- he says he doesn't believe. However, there is still a possibility that he might be able to if I show him the map. If he can't with the map in front of him, then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Show it to him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If the -- if the middle bottom part could be enlarged, please. And maybe scrolled up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you want me to enlarge the map further or are you able to roughly point out your location where you were for ten days?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Please believe me, I never worked with maps, so it's very hard for me to find my way around a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I'll then show you a photograph. If I can have 65 ter 3352 brought up on the screen, please. And if this could not be broadcast, since it is an exhibit from the Galic case under seal. Can the photograph be enlarged; is that possible? Now, Witness, this is a photograph taken from Ozrenska Street, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's possible, but I was never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And from this position, you can see the city of Sarajevo down there, can't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And during the conflict there was a position here with soldiers -- SRK soldiers with rifles. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you will see that in the photograph there is a red circle. Do you see that red circle?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I think if you look closely, that red circle -- well, I'm suggesting to you that the red circle indicates where a transversal or a cross-roads in the city existed. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The town was full of cross-roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But what's in this location in the circle is just one of those cross-roads. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, that soldiers with rifles from this location targeted civilians crossing at that point, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would like to see a soldier who would hit a civilian from this distance from a rifle. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So can you just answer my question. Were civilians targeted at that cross-roads from this position, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this is probably the 20th question that has to do with civilians and the deliberate firing at civilians. So far he has at least given 15 answers about that, and now again the question is repeated, whereas he talked about the attitude that at least was his in terms of civilians. I'm not mistaken if I say that this is the 10th or the 15th time that the same question is being put to the witness. And he answered the previous question that it was impossible for anyone to be hit from that place from that distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, is there another repetition?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, but I suggest to you that it would be possible if there were weapons with optical sights on them or if binoculars were used. I'm not saying it happened, but people could be engaged from this distance, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am telling you that I would place myself in that position and a world championship in marksmanship would not be able to hit me. We were not able to stand up to make a shot like that, because the lines were right next to us in the houses that you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think you've answered my question. My suggestion to you is that if there were optical sights on these rifles or if binoculars were used, persons could be engaged from that location. Do you agree or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I disagree. You could fire randomly, but you wouldn't be able to hit anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So Sarajevo-Romanija Corps soldiers would fire randomly from this position, I suggest to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I said it's possible to fire, but since the lines were extremely close together, you can see where these houses are. There was nobody who dared stand up and fire from that place because they would be seen. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I ask that this photograph be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as P806, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, just a last couple of questions now. You remember you told the Court that there were -- that there were cross-roads in the town of Sarajevo. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The city is full of cross-roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you're aware that at these cross-roads there were protective barriers or containers erected there. You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And these protective barriers or containers were there to protect civilians, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, as it was on our side, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on -- at least on the cross-roads within the territory of the ABiH in Sarajevo, they were erected there because civilians were occasionally hit by fire from the SRK. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In some cases, it was propaganda as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But in some cases, civilians were hit from fire from the SRK, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the number of questions to which the witness has answered increases, concerning the targeting of civilians. He was quite specific about it and for ten or 15 times he's tried to answer it. This is just another way to put the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is in a different context, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, will you answer my question? I'm suggesting to that you in some cases, those cases that you say -- I'm not talking about the cases that you say were propaganda, but in some cases civilians at those cross-roads were hit by fire from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My answer was clear. The same thing was on our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So your answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, do you know of the sky-scrapers at Lenjinova Street?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I -- well, it's right, isn't it, that there were SRK soldiers on those sky-scrapers during the conflict, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You never heard about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you know who Ivkovic Nebojsa was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How about Marinko Krneta?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How about Zeljko Jadranic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I did not spend any time in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about those areas. I'm just asking you whether you know these people. How about Milenko Mitric, did you ever hear about him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And how about Dragan Atanakovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just have one second to confer with my colleague, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's the cross-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems I will have a number of questions, but I will try to be as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mandic, throughout those years -- and I'm not making a distinction between the period of time pertaining to Dragomir Milosevic and what preceded that period, but throughout those years did you ever see a written orders that a civilian should be made target?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not only that I did not see such an order, but it was strictly forbidden for us to target civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone ever tell you anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If someone said something like that to you, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would refuse to carry out such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the photograph --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can have P806 shown to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While waiting for the photograph to appear, you said that in your trenches, in your street, three of your co-fighters were killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Ozrenska Street, your street, how many casualties were there among the soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Exceptionally many.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain why, why in that place in particular?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because the separation line or lines were separated by only four to six metres. When the truce came into force on our side, we no longer opened fire. However, the opposing side kept opening fire. They would hit residential buildings and houses were civilians still resided. People would relax in such periods, and what would happened -- happen was that then they would get hit by snipers or mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From these positions, or, rather, you talked about these positions a while ago. You said what would have happened had you tried to stand up. What was happening when you were in places such as this one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Ozrenska Street, we were in trenches only, while the other side was in the houses which were additionally reinforced by some panels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was in the houses that we can see here in the front row?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I withdraw that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What could you see from your trench in a situation such as this one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We could see perhaps one metre above the ground, since we were below it in the trenches. Therefore, I could see from my trench four houses and four trenches in them, whereas we had that one trench only. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When looking at the photograph, the hills in the background --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- which hills are those and who was positioned there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is Hum. All of those hills that we can see were 100 per cent occupied by the AB and H.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us have a look at a prosecution exhibit. That is P802. The date is the 10th of February. Can you tell the Judges what the date is on the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: 10 February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There are three paragraphs there. Can you read the third one on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "The pieces from the 4th" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. It says the Main Staff, General Milovanovic and then the three paragraphs. The last one.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "We are doing this because our commission was required to act upon the agreement reached with the Muslim side on the 9th of February, 1994."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the next day, after the agreement was signed, as would seem from this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What follows under the paragraph you just read out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "The proposal is the following."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you. I won't ask you for your opinion, but if it is stated as such what does it mean in our language. Can you explain this, "the proposal is the following"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "In order to honour the agreement and to withdraw heavy artillery."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was only a proposal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that last question was leading, in my submission, especially in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not so sure, Mr. Sachdeva. But carry on, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we turn to page 2, who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But what does it say? What was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Deputy commander, colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When Dragomir Milosevic assumed the position of commander, concerning the things you said about heavy weaponry, where you were, were things as shown here when it comes to heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. But that time, the heavy weaponry had been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at P803 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I guess you can see the document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 20th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you try and read the handwritten note?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Logistics, check what can be done about this and respond."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look at the text, please look at the second line. What does it say after "brigade"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It says: "Approve the installing."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please read out the last sentence. Igmanska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Igman infantry brigade at RM/V51314SK because in order to produce this new launcher we are still unable to do so, since we are unable to secure the necessary technical materiel."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I won't ask you to make any conclusions as to that. But can one conclude whether the launcher existed at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I conclude, based on this, that they were not in the position to make such a launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at P804. It is a Prosecution Exhibit; the number is P804. I don't have it in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the penultimate paragraph, the biggest one, but in particular its last sentence. Please read out loud.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure which of the two documents you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the date.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 22nd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "In carrying out this order, the command" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Thank you. We don't have the time. What date is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 22nd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the longest paragraph and read out loud the last sentence of it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The last sentence of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Once the launcher," is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Once the launcher has been installed on the selected vehicle, the 1st Motorised Brigade shall take over the launcher from Hadzici RZ and transfer it to the unit."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you recall the previous document and having read this one, was there a launcher in existence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In seems that one was never made, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P805, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The date is what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 25th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go slowly. Let's wait for the document first. What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 25th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Read out loud the last sentence of the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "In addition" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, sorry, my mistake. Start with the word "especially," or "separately." Start with the words "we point out, or we are particularly warning of," and then the rest. Mr. Mandic, you began reading the first sentence. What I'm telling you is do not read the first one but everything that follows. "We are warning" --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "We would like to warn you that due to technical problems in the production, the replenishment with D30 122-millimetre rounds and T55 100-millimetre rounds is not to be expected any time soon."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we looked at the previous document and we have this date the 25th of July and you were also answering to the Prosecutor's questions, during that time what was going on in the area of responsibility of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right at this moment there was a particularly fierce offensive going on in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva -- just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the area of responsibility of the SRK is a huge area and so if my learned friend is asking the witness to talk about activities, for example, in Mrkovici or in Vogosca, I can't see how this witness would know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I wanted to ask him that next. Since he was in Lukavica and it was the time of the very fierce offensive, as he said, what was the situation like in Lukavica, Grbavica, and your immediate environs in June and July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you must wait for me to rule on the objection. The objection has been raised. But ask the witness the question that you just posed to him, the basis of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that the objection was founded, but I wanted to ask the witness what he knows about the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You told me yesterday what sort of operations you participated in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were speaking about an action in which you took part in a street. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I recall it was in Danila Ponjarca street in Dobrinja IV.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then can you please respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, don't respond before we hear from Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, now my objection is, I don't see how this arises out of cross-examination, especially if Mr. Tapuskovic is going back to evidence that he elicited yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see how it arises, either. Put another question, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm only thinking of dealing with the document of the 25th of July and I was about to ask the witness what his knowledge was about the combat actions in the time covered by this document, the 25th of July, 1995, in view of what he said yesterday about June and July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In June and July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, don't answer. I have ruled against it. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, but that was the time of the fiercest clashes on offensive. I can tell the Court that. But I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Take your seat, Mr. Tapuskovic, before you run into trouble. Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I have -- might I change places with my colleague, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly. The next witness, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, Your Honours. The next witness is Rade Ivanovic. I don't have the T number. T-22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as you know, I represent General Dragomir Milosevic, and in order for us to proceed in the best possible way, can we communicate as slowly as possible, and can you please pay attention to the monitor in front of you and please do not begin your answer until everything that I have said is noted in the transcript. I'm also going to take care so that our examination-in-chief can proceed smoothly. Can you please tell the Judges your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Rade Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You can just reply with a yes to the following questions. You were born on the 22nd of November, 1944?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born in Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.
